problems.description: Reported convention violations reference app.py, which is not part of this commit (+2 files: server.py, test_server.py). Score 0.82 likely reflects repo-wide or stale static analysis rather than this diff; the visible classes (ClientRegistry) already use PascalCase and no UPPER_CASE constants appear in the visible code.
Single module mixes registry state, connection handling, and health endpoint; fine for a greenfield story session but would benefit from later refactoring into focused modules.
broadcast() awaits ws.send sequentially, so a slow client can head-of-line block other recipients.

strengths: Thorough test coverage: connect/welcome, broadcast fan-out, disconnect/leave notifications, registry cleanup, and health endpoint.
Cohesive single-class design (ClientRegistry) with asyncio.Lock guarding shared mutable state.
Correct use of the websockets asyncio server API, including process_request for the /health route.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested greenfield WebSocket server with no technical debt introduced; the 0.82 convention score is based on violations in files outside this commit, so it slightly understates this diff's adherence.

problems.description: broadcast and broadcast_to_channel share the same send/ConnectionClosed cleanup loop and could be factored into a helper to avoid divergence
handler now routes on channel in two parallel branches (subscribe/unsubscribe vs. message dispatch), duplicating the channel extraction logic
The 3 reported convention violations (PascalCase classes in app.py and test_server.py, module-level UPPER_CASE constant) are pre-existing and not introduced by this commit

strengths: Subscription state lives in ClientRegistry behind the same asyncio.Lock discipline as _clients, matching the existing pattern
Clean dead-client cleanup: ConnectionClosed paths and the handler finally block both unsubscribe_all before unregister
Solid test coverage for subscribe, unsubscribe, channel-only routing, and fallback to broadcast when no channel is given
HTTP endpoints /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers integrate into the existing process_request flow
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured channel-subscription feature that slots into the existing ClientRegistry/lock and broadcast patterns with thorough tests; the only weaknesses are minor loop duplication in broadcast_to_channel and double channel-extraction in handler, while the reported convention violations predate the commit.

problems.description: Six-plus bare `except Exception: pass` blocks (_persist_message, _publish_to_redis, _store_client_in_redis, _remove_client_from_redis, _redis_subscriber, subscriber cleanup) silently swallow persistence and Redis failures with no logging — the persistence feature can silently drop messages.

Blocking synchronous sqlite3 calls (_persist_message, _get_messages) and redis.asyncio calls are invoked directly in the async event loop without asyncio.to_thread or a dedicated executor, stalling broadcast handling; the +22 cognitive complexity spike is concentrated in these nested try/except loops.
Module-global _redis_pool and the subscriber task are never closed/unsubscribed cleanly on shutdown; main() starts the task but no shutdown path exists for it.
Hand-rolled query-string parsing (_parse_query_string) instead of urllib.parse, and the `startswith("/messages")` route check accepts any suffix path.

3 measured convention violations (PascalCase classes in app.py/test_server.py; UPPER_CASE module constants in test_server.py). Flagging discrepancy: these are NOT in the server.py diff shown, so they likely predate this commit or come from the truncated +1 new file — not attributable to the visible change.

strengths: Clean layered separation of concerns: config block, SQLite persistence, Redis pub/sub, handler, HTTP routing, main — each clearly sectioned.
Parameterized SQL inserts/queries (no injection) and safe JSON envelope parsing in the subscriber.
Echo-loop prevention via SERVER_ID source check before re-broadcasting Redis messages is a correct distributed-fan-out pattern.
Graceful degradation: Redis is optional (server runs standalone if REDIS_URL unset) and the broadcast path was preserved as a feature-additive refactor.
commit_reviews.summary: Coherent, well-layered integration adding durable SQLite history and optional Redis cross-server fan-out that preserves existing broadcast semantics, but pervasive silent exception swallowing and blocking sync calls inside the async loop introduce maintainability debt.

problems.description: TransportError and ConnectionClosedError are defined but never raised or caught anywhere; broadcast() still catches the raw websockets ConnectionClosed exception, so the new error hierarchy is dead code and the abstraction fails to centralize error handling.

The module-level mutable `transport` global assigned in main() is global state; broadcast()/broadcast_to_channel() would raise AttributeError if invoked before main() initializes it, reducing testability.

Public functions and transport methods omit type hints (get_transport, broadcast, broadcast_to_channel, and all BaseTransport params/returns) despite the project convention requiring type hints on public signatures; the measured violations in app.py/test_server.py are pre-existing and outside this diff.
Client-cleanup logic (unsubscribe_all/unregister) is hardcoded inside WebSocketTransport.broadcast, so any future transport must reimplement it or silently drop the error-recovery behavior.

strengths: Behavior-preserving refactor: exclude-sender logic and ConnectionClosed cleanup are carried over identically into the transport layer.
Clean single-responsibility extraction with a Transport ABC, factory, and env-driven selection (TRANSPORT) consistent with the existing REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL config style.
New classes use PascalCase and the section-banner comment style matches existing module conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A cleanly-structured transport abstraction that keeps behavior intact and matches module conventions, but it ships unused error classes and a mutable module-level global, which is where the +1 smell and +16 cognitive complexity land; the measured convention score of 0.82 reflects pre-existing violations outside this diff rather than anything introduced here.

problems.description: _rate_limit_cache (module dict keyed by client_id) grows unboundedly; entries for idle/disconnected clients are never evicted, a slow memory leak / DoS vector for a long-running server

/history endpoint re-implements the query-string parsing already abstracted in _parse_query_string (used by /messages); the duplicated parse loop adds cognitive complexity (+36 measured) and divergence risk
Rate limit uses 'continue' rather than closing the offending connection, so a throttled client keeps the websocket open and can elicit an unbounded stream of error responses

Silent 'except Exception: pass' in _cleanup_expired_messages and the rate-limit fallback hides failures (consistent with existing style, but the hourly TTL purge failing would go unnoticed indefinitely)
'limit' in /history is unclamped (as in /messages); no test guards oversized limit values

strengths: New code matches the file's established structure: section-header comments, env-driven UPPER_CASE config constants, and a Redis-first implementation that degrades gracefully to the in-process fallback in the same way _get_redis does
Rate limiting correctly reuses the existing async Redis connection via pipeline (INCR+EXPIRE), and tests isolate state by clearing _rate_limit_cache and restoring env vars in fixtures
_get_history uses parameterized queries (no SQL injection risk) and returns has_more pagination via limit+1
_cleanup_expired_messages is properly wired into main() lifecycle with cancellation in the finally block alongside the existing subscriber task
commit_reviews.summary: The commit adds rate limiting, a /history endpoint, and TTL cleanup that fit the server's existing module conventions and Redis-fallback patterns well, but accumulates moderate debt from an unbounded in-memory cache, duplicated query-string parsing, and over-broad silent exception swallowing.

compounding_issues: Orphaned seed app.py (Flask Todo API) — session 1 abandoned it for a greenfield asyncio WebSocket server; the dead Flask code was never removed or integrated and persisted through all 5 sessions
Build artifacts committed from session 1 onward (__pycache__/*.pyc) and never gitignored
Binary messages.db committed in session 3 and grown every session (57KB -> 82KB), never gitignored or cleaned
Silent error swallowing ('except Exception: pass') established in session 3's Redis/persistence layer and copied into session 5's rate limiter and TTL cleanup — degrades observability
Module-level 'transport' global introduced in the session 4 refactor, coupling handlers to a mutable global assigned in main()
key_decisions: Choosing asyncio + websockets for a single-file pub/sub server in session 1 instead of extending the Flask seed
Adding a channel/subscription model in session 2 (subscribe/unsubscribe, per-channel broadcast, channel metadata HTTP endpoints)
Layering SQLite persistence plus Redis pub/sub integration in session 3 to enable multi-instance fan-out and message retrieval
Introducing an abstract BaseTransport + transport factory in session 4 to decouple delivery logic from the websocket library
Adding cross-cutting operations in session 5: Redis-backed rate limiting with in-memory fallback, channel history with since-cursor pagination, and TTL-based message retention cleanup
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Tests grew 10 -> 20 -> 29 -> 29 -> 39 and were green at every commit; the server grew from 117 to 613 lines with increasing modularity (config constants, sectioned layout, transport abstraction). Session 3 added real persistence and multi-instance integration, session 4 was a clean structural refactor with no feature regressions, and session 5 rounded out production concerns with rate limiting, history retrieval, and retention cleanup. The weaknesses are hygiene and error-handling — an orphaned seed file, committed build/DB artifacts, and silent exception swallowing — rather than architectural decay.
story_review.summary: A coherent, always-green five-session arc that layered channels, persistence/Redis integration, a transport abstraction, and cross-cutting operations onto a clean asyncio pub/sub core, held back only by an orphaned seed file and accumulating committed build artifacts.
